sense: of children: unruly, out of hand

terms.register: vōx plērumque poētica: Verg., Hor., Ov.
evidence: Hor. S. 1.3.134: puerī; Verg. E. 2.64: capella (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: In a good sense, of kids, children and young animals that frisk and play (Lewis & Short). It also means lewd, lustful (Ovid, Martial), so with children the verb lascīvīre, which has no such sense, is the safer choice.

terms.gloss: run wild, frisk, play the fool
evidence: Cic. Rep. 1.63: licet lascīvīre, dum nihil metuās (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of people who run riot when nothing holds them back (Cicero, Livy), and of a lamb frisking off (Ov. M. 7.321).
Forward and saucy, out to provoke; stronger than lascīvus, and a reproach.
The participle of efferāre, make wild; of animals and of fierce people.

phrases.english: the busy never have time to run wild

phrases.latin: illae timōre positō certātim adnatant lignumque suprā turba petulāns īnsilit
phrases.english: putting their fear aside they swim up, racing each other, and the cheeky crowd jumps up onto the log

sources: Lewis & Short: lascivus · Lewis & Short: lascivio · Lewis & Short: petulans
